questions.stem: Macedon, Alexander's homeland, lay:
options: north of Thessaly, with fertile plains, timber and access to mines in Thrace
in the Peloponnese, between Sparta and Corinth, on a dry and rocky upland plain
on the coast of Asia Minor, opposite the island of Lesbos and near Troy
on the island of Crete, controlling the sea routes to Egypt and Cyprus
questions.explanation: Macedon lay in northern Greece. Its plains, timber for ships and, after Philip's conquests, the gold and silver mines near Mount Pangaeum gave it great resources.

questions.stem: The sarissa, central to Philip II's reformed Macedonian phalanx, was:
options: a heavy bronze shield that covered a soldier from chin to knee
a torsion catapult used by engineers to break down the walls of besieged cities
a long pike, much longer than a hoplite's spear, held with both hands
a short curved sword used by cavalry to cut down fleeing infantry
questions.explanation: The sarissa was a pike of around five to six metres. With it, the front ranks of the phalanx presented a hedge of points ahead of enemy spears.

questions.stem: How did Philip II's reforms change the way the Macedonian army fought?
options: The cavalry was disbanded so that all men could fight on foot in hoplite ranks
The army relied on hired Greek hoplites, with Macedonians serving only as archers
The army fought only from behind field walls, never attacking in the open
The phalanx held the enemy while heavy Companion cavalry struck the decisive blow
questions.explanation: Philip combined a pike phalanx, the Companion cavalry, the hypaspists and light troops, with siege engineers and year-round training. This 'hammer and anvil' system was the army Alexander inherited.

questions.stem: Alexander's parents were:
options: Philip II of Macedon and Cleopatra, the niece of Attalus
Amyntas III of Macedon and Eurydice, a princess of Illyria
Darius III of Persia and Stateira, his Persian queen
Philip II of Macedon and Olympias, a princess of Epirus
questions.explanation: Alexander was born in 356 BCE to Philip and Olympias, a princess of the Molossians of Epirus. Cleopatra was Philip's last wife, and Amyntas III and Eurydice were Philip's parents.

questions.stem: From about 343 BCE, Alexander was taught at Mieza by:
options: Herodotus
Aristotle
Plato
Socrates
questions.explanation: Philip hired Aristotle to teach Alexander and other young Macedonians at Mieza. Socrates and Herodotus were long dead, and Plato died in 347 BCE.

questions.stem: At the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, the eighteen-year-old Alexander:
options: commanded the Macedonian fleet that blockaded the harbour of Athens
was left in Pella as regent and took no part in the fighting at all
led the Athenian contingent, since he had been raised as a hostage there
commanded the Macedonian left wing, which broke the Theban Sacred Band
questions.explanation: Philip's victory over Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea gave Macedon control of Greece. His success against the Sacred Band showed his early ability as a commander.

questions.stem: Philip's marriage to Cleopatra, niece of the noble Attalus, threatened Alexander's position because:
options: Attalus was the commander of the Companion cavalry and refused to serve Alexander
a son by a Macedonian noblewoman might be preferred as a fully Macedonian heir
Cleopatra was already the mother of an adult son who had been named Philip's heir
Macedonian law forbade a king's son from inheriting if his father remarried
questions.explanation: Plutarch says Attalus prayed at the wedding for a legitimate heir, provoking Alexander. Alexander and Olympias left the court for a time, showing how insecure the succession had become.

questions.stem: Philip II was assassinated in 336 BCE at Aegae, during a royal wedding, by:
options: Attalus, the uncle of his last wife
Demosthenes, the Athenian orator
Bessus, the satrap of Bactria
Pausanias, one of his own bodyguards
questions.explanation: Pausanias, a member of the bodyguard, stabbed Philip and was killed as he fled. Ancient writers suspected Olympias, Alexander or Persia of involvement, but nothing was proved.

questions.stem: After Philip's death, Alexander secured his throne by:
options: calling an assembly of all Greeks to vote him their king
winning the army's support and removing rivals such as Attalus
sharing the kingdom with his half-brother and ruling jointly
asking the Persian king to recognise him as satrap of Macedon
questions.explanation: Alexander was acclaimed by the army, had Attalus killed and removed other possible claimants such as his cousin Amyntas. Speed and ruthlessness kept the throne secure.

questions.stem: In 335 BCE Thebes revolted on a false report that Alexander was dead. How did Alexander respond?
options: He pardoned the Thebans and made their leaders his advisers on the Persian war
He ignored the revolt and crossed to Asia, leaving Antipater to deal with it
He moved his capital to Thebes so that he could watch over central Greece
He destroyed the city and enslaved its people, warning the other Greek states
questions.explanation: Thebes was razed except for its temples and the house of the poet Pindar, and its people were sold into slavery. Athens and other states quickly submitted.

questions.stem: As leader (hegemon) of the League of Corinth, Alexander justified the war against Persia as:
options: revenge for the Persian invasions of Greece and the burning of temples
a campaign to restore democracy in every Greek city of the Persian Empire
a defence of Macedon against a Persian army already marching west
a crusade to spread the worship of Zeus to the peoples of Asia
questions.explanation: The war was presented as a panhellenic war of revenge for Xerxes' invasion. That theme was later used to explain the burning of Persepolis.

questions.stem: Which order of Alexander's major battles is correct?
options: Issus, Granicus, Hydaspes, Gaugamela
Gaugamela, Granicus, Issus, Hydaspes
Granicus, Gaugamela, Issus, Hydaspes
Granicus, Issus, Gaugamela, Hydaspes
questions.explanation: Granicus was fought in 334 BCE, Issus in 333 BCE, Gaugamela in 331 BCE and the Hydaspes in 326 BCE.

questions.stem: At the Granicus River in 334 BCE, Alexander faced:
options: Darius III in person, leading the full royal army of the Persian Empire
the Indian king Porus, whose army included many war elephants
the army of the Greek cities of Ionia, which had sided with Persia
the forces of the Persian satraps of Asia Minor, with Greek mercenaries
questions.explanation: The satraps of western Asia Minor tried to stop Alexander at the river. Darius III first met him in person at Issus the next year.

questions.stem: After Issus in 333 BCE, Darius III fled and Alexander captured:
options: Darius himself, whom he held prisoner until his death in Babylon
Darius's mother, wife and children, whom he treated with respect
Darius's capital at Persepolis, which he burned the next morning
the Persian fleet, which surrendered to him at the harbour of Tyre
questions.explanation: The royal women fell into Alexander's hands in the Persian camp, and the ancient sources stress his courteous treatment of them. Darius escaped and was killed in 330 BCE by his own satrap Bessus.

questions.stem: Alexander besieged Tyre for about seven months in 332 BCE. Why did he not simply bypass the island city?
options: The oracle at Delphi had told him that Asia would fall only after Tyre
The Tyrians had captured and executed his envoys at the Granicus River
He needed to deny the Persian fleet its bases before he moved further east
Tyre was sheltering Darius III, who had fled there after his defeat at Gaugamela
questions.explanation: By taking the Phoenician ports, Alexander defeated the Persian navy from the land. He built a mole out to the island and used ships with siege engines to break in.

questions.stem: In Egypt in 331 BCE, Alexander visited the oracle of Ammon at Siwa. What did this visit contribute to his image?
options: Claims that he was the son of Ammon, identified by Greeks with Zeus
A crown of Upper Egypt that made him king of Egypt and Nubia alone
A prophecy that he would die young, which made him avoid battle
A treaty with Egypt that kept it independent of the Persian Empire
questions.explanation: The sources say the priest greeted him as son of Ammon. Coins later showed Alexander with ram's horns, the symbol of Zeus Ammon.

questions.stem: At Gaugamela in 331 BCE, Darius chose a level plain, even smoothing the ground for his scythed chariots. How did Alexander win?
options: He used war elephants captured at Issus to trample the Persian cavalry
He drew the Persian line to his right, then charged into a gap that opened in it
He attacked at night, so the Persians could not see where his troops were placed
He refused battle and starved the Persian army until it broke up on its own
questions.explanation: Alexander moved obliquely to his right, pulling Persian cavalry after him, then led the Companions into the gap in Darius's centre. Darius fled. Alexander rejected a night attack, saying he would not steal a victory.

questions.stem: At the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, Alexander faced Porus across a swollen river. Which tactic gave him victory?
options: He built a bridge of boats under the cover of catapults on the opposite bank
He waited for the river to dry up in late summer and then crossed with his whole army
He made repeated feints, then crossed upstream secretly by night with part of his army
He bribed Porus's generals to desert, so that the Indian army had no commanders
questions.explanation: By staging false crossings, Alexander made Porus stop reacting, then crossed some distance upstream in a storm. His cavalry and phalanx defeated Porus's army and elephants, and Porus was kept on as a ruler.

questions.stem: Alexander usually led the Companion cavalry in person at the decisive point of a battle. What was a disadvantage of this style of leadership?
options: He could not be seen by his troops, who therefore lost heart in battle
He left the cavalry without orders, since he fought only with the phalanx
He had to stay far behind the line, too distant to change his plans
He was often badly wounded, risking the whole campaign on his survival
questions.explanation: Alexander was wounded many times, most seriously at the town of the Malli in India. His death would have left the army leaderless far from home.

questions.stem: After Gaugamela, Alexander often appointed Persian nobles as satraps. Why?
options: Because his own generals refused to stay in Asia after the war ended
To prepare the Persian provinces for independence after his death
To win the loyalty of the Persian elite and use their experience of government
Because Macedonian law forbade Macedonians from serving as provincial governors abroad
questions.explanation: Persians such as Mazaeus, made satrap of Babylon, kept their posts, though Macedonians often controlled troops and finance. The policy was practical, but it angered some Macedonians.

questions.stem: Alexandria in Egypt was significant because it:
options: was the city where Alexander defeated Porus and his elephants
became a great port and centre of Greek learning under the Ptolemies
was the city where Alexander was born and where his father Philip ruled
was the Persian capital where Alexander found the royal treasury
questions.explanation: Alexander founded Alexandria on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt. Under the Ptolemies it became a capital with the famous Library and Museum. Alexander founded many other cities, often named after himself.

questions.stem: In 324 BCE at Susa, Alexander and dozens of his Companions married Persian and other Iranian noblewomen. The most likely aim was to:
options: reward his officers with dowries, since the treasuries were empty
bind the Macedonian and Persian elites together in ruling the empire
end the war with Persia, since Darius III was still alive and resisting
satisfy Macedonian custom, which required kings to marry foreign brides
questions.explanation: Alexander married Stateira, a daughter of Darius III, and Parysatis. Most of the Companions abandoned their Persian wives after his death, showing how unpopular the policy was.

questions.stem: Alexander's first wife, whom he married in 327 BCE, was:
options: Barsine, the widow of Memnon of Rhodes
Olympias, the princess of Epirus
Roxane, the daughter of a Bactrian noble
Stateira, the daughter of Darius III
questions.explanation: Roxane was the daughter of Oxyartes, a Sogdian or Bactrian noble. The marriage helped secure the north-east. Her son, Alexander IV, was born after Alexander's death.

questions.stem: Alexander began wearing some items of Persian royal dress and trained 30,000 Iranian youths, the Epigoni, in Macedonian fighting. How did many Macedonians react?
options: They resented it as favouring Persians and turning their king into an eastern despot
They welcomed it, since it meant they could go home and leave the fighting to others
They copied it, adopting Persian dress and language throughout the whole army
They took no notice, since Alexander made the changes only in private
questions.explanation: These policies fed the resentment that came out in the mutiny at Opis in 324 BCE, where the veterans complained they were being replaced.

questions.stem: At the Hyphasis (Beas) River in 326 BCE:
options: the army refused to march further east, and Alexander had to turn back
Alexander defeated the Indian king Porus in a battle against elephants
Alexander founded a city named after his horse Bucephalus's birthplace
the Persian nobles rebelled and tried to make Bessus king in his place
questions.explanation: After years of campaigning, the men would go no further. Coenus spoke for them and Alexander, after sulking in his tent, agreed to return. It was his first defeat, at the hands of his own army.

questions.stem: At Opis in 324 BCE, Alexander announced that veterans unfit for service would be sent home. The army mutinied, and Alexander gave Persians commands and Macedonian unit names. What does the outcome show?
options: The Persians overthrew the Macedonians and took control of the empire
The veterans killed their officers and marched home without permission
The army depended on him as much as he on it, and they were reconciled
Alexander lost control of the army and was forced to abdicate as king
questions.explanation: The Macedonians gave way when they saw Persians being honoured in their place, and a great banquet of reconciliation followed. The veterans then went home under Craterus.

questions.stem: In 330 BCE Philotas, commander of the Companion cavalry, was executed for failing to report a plot, and his father Parmenion was then killed in Media. Why was Parmenion killed?
options: Parmenion had been found guilty of plotting to murder Alexander by a Persian court
Parmenion had lost the Battle of Gaugamela by refusing to obey Alexander's orders
Parmenion had tried to make himself king of Macedon while Alexander was in Asia
Alexander feared he would seek revenge with the troops and treasury under his command
questions.explanation: No trial was held for Parmenion. As Philip's senior general, he held large forces and the treasury at Ecbatana, so after his son's death Alexander saw him as a danger.

questions.stem: At Maracanda in 328 BCE, during a drunken quarrel, Alexander killed Cleitus the Black. What had Cleitus done?
options: Lost a battle against the Scythians by ignoring Alexander's orders
Criticised Alexander's eastern ways and praised the deeds of Philip and the veterans
Plotted with a group of Persian nobles to poison Alexander during the banquet that night
Refused to cross the Hindu Kush and led the cavalry back to Macedon
questions.explanation: Cleitus, who had saved Alexander's life at the Granicus, mocked the flattery of the court and the king's claims. Alexander speared him and then grieved bitterly.

questions.stem: In 327 BCE Alexander tried to introduce proskynesis, the Persian practice of bowing or prostrating before the king, among his Greeks and Macedonians. Why did it fail?
options: Greeks saw it as fit only for gods, and Callisthenes publicly refused
Persians refused it, saying that Alexander was not a true Persian king
The army was in India and could not reach the court at the time
Aristotle wrote to Alexander forbidding him to accept it from anyone
questions.explanation: For Persians it was a sign of respect to a superior, but Greeks associated it with worship. After Callisthenes' refusal, Alexander dropped it. Callisthenes was later accused in the Pages' conspiracy and died in captivity.

questions.stem: Hephaestion, whose death in 324 BCE devastated Alexander, was:
options: the Athenian orator who opposed Macedon
the regent left in charge of Macedon
his closest friend and a senior commander
the Persian satrap who killed Darius III
questions.explanation: Hephaestion was Alexander's lifelong friend, later chiliarch and husband of Darius's daughter Drypetis. Antipater was regent in Macedon and Demosthenes the Athenian orator.

questions.stem: Alexander died in June 323 BCE at:
options: Susa, aged 36
Babylon, aged 32
Persepolis, aged 40
Pella, aged 25
questions.explanation: Alexander died at Babylon after a fever of about ten days, before a planned campaign in Arabia. He was not yet 33.

questions.stem: Why do historians still debate the cause of Alexander's death?
options: No ancient writer recorded where or when he died, so it is unknown
The sources record both an illness and rumours of poisoning, with no clear proof
His body was examined by several Greek doctors who left conflicting written reports
His tomb was opened in modern times and showed signs of a battle wound
questions.explanation: The royal journals cited by Arrian and Plutarch describe a fever, while other writers report a poisoning plot linked to Antipater's sons. Modern suggestions include malaria and typhoid.

questions.stem: What was the main impact of Alexander's death on his empire?
options: His generals, the Successors, fought for decades and divided it into kingdoms
His son ruled peacefully for forty years with Roxane as his regent
The Persian royal family regained the throne and expelled the Greeks
Athens took control of the whole empire under the leadership of the orator Demosthenes
questions.explanation: With no adult heir, the Successors (Diadochi) such as Ptolemy, Seleucus and Antigonus fought over the empire. Alexander's son and half-brother were both killed.

questions.stem: Arrian's Anabasis, the main narrative of Alexander's campaigns, was written:
options: in the fifth century CE by a Christian bishop in Alexandria
in the second century CE, based on Ptolemy and Aristobulus
during Alexander's lifetime by his official court historian
in the fourth century BCE by a soldier in Alexander's army
questions.explanation: Arrian wrote about four and a half centuries after Alexander, preferring the lost accounts of Ptolemy and Aristobulus, who had served with him. No contemporary account survives complete.

questions.stem: Arrian relied mainly on Ptolemy, who served with Alexander and later became king of Egypt. What is a likely limitation of this source?
options: Ptolemy was an enemy of Alexander and wrote only to blacken his name
Ptolemy may have stressed his own role and his loyalty to Alexander
Ptolemy never met Alexander and had to rely on rumours from Persia
Ptolemy wrote in Egyptian, so Arrian had to guess at much of the meaning
questions.explanation: Ptolemy held Alexander's body in Egypt and drew legitimacy from him, so he had reasons to show both Alexander and himself favourably. The so-called 'vulgate' tradition, as in Curtius, is more critical.

questions.stem: The 'Alexander Mosaic' from the House of the Faun at Pompeii shows Alexander charging towards Darius in his chariot. What does it tell historians?
options: That Darius was killed by Alexander in person during the battle
That the painting was copied from a photograph of the battlefield
How Alexander was imagined and celebrated long after his death
Exactly how the armies were arranged at the start of Gaugamela
questions.explanation: The mosaic, probably based on a Hellenistic painting, shows a heroic image of Alexander facing Darius. It is evidence of his later reputation more than of battle details.

questions.stem: W. W. Tarn presented Alexander as an idealist who dreamed of the unity of mankind, while Ernst Badian and A. B. Bosworth stressed his ruthlessness. What best explains such different views?
options: Historians weigh the sources differently and are shaped by the ideas of their own times
Tarn used Persian sources unknown to Badian, which proved his kinder interpretation
Badian and Bosworth wrote before archaeologists had found evidence of his campaigns
Tarn had access to Alexander's own memoirs, which were lost before Badian wrote
questions.explanation: Tarn wrote in an age that admired empire-builders and emphasised the Opis banquet. Later historians, writing after the world wars, focused on the killings of Philotas, Parmenion and Cleitus and the cost of conquest.

questions.stem: Which judgement of Alexander's impact is best supported by the evidence?
options: He ruined Greek culture by replacing the Greek language with Persian
He had little lasting effect, since his empire fell back to Persia at once
He spread Greek culture and cities across the east, but left no stable succession
He created a united empire that lasted for several centuries under his descendants
questions.explanation: The Hellenistic kingdoms, Greek cities such as Alexandria, and Greek as a common language in the east grew out of his conquests. Yet his empire broke apart within a generation of his death.
